claim: High-resolution Hi-C data from early Drosophila embryos was generated.
source: Here we present high resolution Hi-C data from early Drosophila embryos.
evidence: The manuscript describes the generation of Hi-C datasets from nuclear cycle 14 Drosophila melanogaster embryos.

claim: Boundaries between topological domains map to DNA elements that resemble classical insulator elements.
source: We demonstrate that boundaries between topological domains of various sizes map to DNA elements that resemble classical insulator elements: short genomic regions sensitive to DNase digestion that are strongly bound by known insulator proteins and are frequently located between divergent promoters.
evidence: The manuscript presents Hi-C data and ChIP data showing that TAD boundaries correspond to short DNase-sensitive regions bound by insulator proteins.

claim: Boundary elements correspond to polytene interband regions.
source: Further, we show a striking correspondence between these elements and the locations of mapped polytene interband regions.
evidence: The manuscript compares Hi-C data with polytene chromosome mapping data from Vatolina et al., showing correspondence between boundaries and interbands.

claim: Decompaction of boundary-insulator-interband regions drives the organization of interphase chromosomes by creating stable physical separation between adjacent domains.
source: We therefore propose a model in which decompaction of boundary-insulator-interband regions drives the organization of interphase chromosomes by creating stable physical separation between adjacent domains.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed correspondence between boundaries, insulators, and interbands, and their physical properties.

claim: Cytological investigations of polytene chromosomes in the late 19th century implicated the physical structure of interphase chromosomes in their cellular functions.
source: Beginning in the late 19th century, cytological investigations of the polytene chromosomes of insect salivary glands implicated the physical structure of interphase chromosomes in their cellular functions (Balbiani, 1881; Balbiani, 1890; Heitz and Bauer, 1933; King and Beams, 1934; Painter, 1935).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to historical literature.

claim: Polytene chromosomes in Drosophila melanogaster have a stereotyped organization with compacted 'bands' alternating with extended 'interband' regions.
source: Detailed examination of polytene chromosomes in Drosophila melanogaster revealed a stereotyped organization, with compacted, DNA-rich 'bands' alternating with extended, DNA-poor 'interband' regions (Bridges, 1934; Rabinowitz, 1941; Lefevre, 1976; Benyajati and Worcel, 1976; Laird and Chooi, 1976a)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies of polytene chromosomes.

claim: Insulators were initially identified based on their ability to block the activity of transcriptional enhancers when located between an enhancer and its targeted promoters.
source: A critical clue came with the discovery of insulators, DNA elements initially identified based on their ability to block the activity of transcriptional enhancers when located between an enhancer and its targeted promoters (Kellum and Schedl, 1991; Holdridge and Dorsett, 1991; Geyer and Corces, 1992; Kellum and Schedl, 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to the original insulator discovery papers.

claim: Insulator elements can block the spread of silenced chromatin states.
source: Subsequent work showed that these elements could also block the spread of silenced chromatin states (Roseman et al., 1993; Sigrist and Pirrotta, 1997; Mallin et al., 1998; Recillas-Targa et al., 2002; Kahn et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating this function of insulators.

claim: Many insulator proteins localize to polytene interbands.
source: Staining of polytene chromosomes with antibodies against such insulator proteins showed that many of them localize to polytene interbands (Belyaeva and Zhimulev, 1994; Zhao et al., 1995; Byrd and Corces, 2003; Eggert et al., 2004; Pai et al., 2004; Gortchakov et al., 2005; Gilbert et al., 2006; Berkaeva et al., 2009; Vatolina et al., 2011b)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to immunostaining studies.

claim: Some insulator protein mutants disrupt polytene chromosome structure.
source: Further, some, though not all, insulator protein mutants disrupt polytene chromosome structure (Roy et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a genetic study.

claim: Fly chromosomes are organized into topologically associated domains (TADs).
source: Several groups have performed Hi-C on Drosophila tissues or cells and have shown that fly chromosomes, like those of other species, are organized into topologically associated domains (TADs), regions within which loci show enriched 3C linkages with each other but depleted linkages with loci outside the domain.
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to prior Hi-C studies in Drosophila.

claim: Disruption of TAD structures by gene editing in mammalian cells significantly alters transcriptional activity.
source: Disruption of TAD structures by gene editing in mammalian cells has been shown to disrupt enhancer-promoter interactions and significantly alter transcriptional activity (Guo et al., 2015; Lupiáñez et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to gene editing studies in mammalian cells.

claim: There is a correspondence between the distribution of large TADs and polytene bands in D. melanogaster.
source: Tantalizingly, Eagen et al., using 15 kb resolution Hi-C data from D. melanogaster have shown that there is a correspondence between the distribution of large TADs and polytene bands (Eagen et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eagen et al., 2015.

claim: Approximately 452 million informative read pairs were produced from Hi-C experiments.
source: In total, we produced ~452 million informative read pairs (see Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the data generated in the study.

claim: The strand orientations of reads were approximately equal in each sample.
source: Specifically, the strand orientations of our reads were approximately equal in each sample (as expected from correct Hi-C libraries but not background genomic sequence; see Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is a quality control metric reported from the Hi-C data analysis.

claim: The prominent 'X' patterns for chromosomes 2 and 3 reflect the Rabl configuration of fly chromosomes during early development.
source: The prominent 'X' patterns for chromosomes 2 and 3, which indicate an enrichment of linkages between chromosome arms, reflects the known organization of fly chromosomes during early development known as the Rabl configuration (Csink and Henikoff, 1998; Wilkie et al., 1999; Duan et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Hi-C heatmaps (Figure 1) and is supported by citations to prior studies describing the Rabl configuration.

claim: Centromeres and the predominantly heterochromatic chromosome 4 cluster together in early Drosophila embryos.
source: Centromeres and the predominantly heterochromatic chromosome 4 cluster together, as, to a lesser extent, do telomeres, reflecting established cytological features that have been detected by prior Hi-C analysis (Sexton et al., 2012) and fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH) (Lowenstein et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is based on Hi-C data (Figure 1) and is supported by citations to prior Hi-C and FISH studies.

claim: TAD boundaries are formed by short regions of DNA (500–2000 bp) that are nearly always associated with high chromatin accessibility and strong occupancy by known insulator proteins.
source: When we compared maps for several of these regions with available functional genomic data from embryos, we observed that the boundaries between these domains showed a remarkably consistent pattern: they were formed by short regions of DNA (500–2000 bp) that are nearly always associated with high chromatin accessibility, measured by DNase-seq (Li et al., 2011), strong occupancy by known insulator proteins as measured by chromatin immunoprecipitation (ChIP) (Nègre et al., 2010) (Figure 2, Figure 2—figure supplements 1–5) properties characteristic of classical Drosophila insulator elements.
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Hi-C maps overlaid with DNase-seq and ChIP-seq data (Figure 2 and supplements).

claim: 3122 boundaries were manually called in the genome for nc14 embryos.
source: In total, we manually called 3122 boundaries in the genome for nc14 embryos.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of boundaries identified by manual curation.

claim: 4000–5500 is a reasonable estimate for the number of boundaries in the genome.
source: Taking into account the ambiguity associated with intrinsically noisy data, the difficulty of resolving small domains, and the invisibility of sections of the genome due to repeat content or a lack of MboI cut sites, we consider 4000–5500 to be a reasonable estimate for the number of boundaries in the genome.
evidence: This is an estimate based on the manual curation and consideration of technical limitations.

claim: Of the top 1000 computationally-identified domain boundaries, 952 were matched by a manually-called boundary within 1 kb.
source: Of our top 1000 computationally-identified domain boundaries, we found that 952 were matched by a manually-called boundary within 1 kb.
evidence: This is a direct comparison of computational and manual boundary calls.

claim: 95.1% of examined boundaries are associated with CP190 binding.
source: CP190 and BEAF-32 show the strongest enrichment, and indeed, virtually all (95.1%) of the examined boundaries appear to be associated with CP190 binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of ChIP-seq data at boundaries (Figure 3 and supplements).

claim: RNA polII is present at only 45.1% of stage 5 boundaries.
source: Despite the presence of promoter marks, we find that RNA polII is present at only a subset (45.1%) of stage 5 boundaries (Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of RNA polII ChIP-seq data at boundaries (Figure 3).

claim: Of the strongest 1000 CP190 peaks, 75.2% are within 2 kb of a manual or computationally-called boundary.
source: Conversely, of the strongest 1000 CP190 peaks, 75.2% are within 2 kb of a manual or computationally-called boundary (compared to 37.4% of the top 1000 RNAPII peaks).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of the overlap between CP190 peaks and boundaries.

claim: A small subset of boundaries (~1–2%) show no enrichment for CP190, BEAF-32, or dCTCF.
source: It is important to note that we do identify a small subset of boundaries that are not apparently associated with sites of insulator binding (~1–2% show no enrichment for CP190, BEAF-32, or dCTCF, depending on thresholds used)
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of insulator protein binding at boundaries.

claim: Many topological boundaries (54.9%) are not associated with RNAPII binding in nc14 embryos.
source: First and most critically, many of the topological boundaries (54.9%) we identify are not associated with RNAPII binding in nc14 embryos.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of RNA polII ChIP-seq data at boundaries.

claim: There are many active promoters that do not appear to form topological boundaries.
source: Similarly, there are many active promoters that do not appear to form topological boundaries (e.g., Figure 8 and supplements).
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Hi-C maps at active promoters (Figure 8 and supplements).

claim: Hug et al., 2017 pharmacologically inhibited transcription in early embryos and observed that TADs remain intact.
source: Hug et al., 2017 pharmacologically inhibited transcription in early embryos and observe that TADs remain intact.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hug et al., 2017.

claim: Topological boundaries are invariant between anterior and posterior sections of embryos despite substantial differences in transcriptional profiles.
source: Finally, topological boundaries are invariant between anterior and posterior sections of embryos despite substantial differences in the transcriptional profiles of these regions (see below).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of Hi-C data from anterior and posterior embryo halves (Figure 7).

claim: The most enriched sequences in boundary elements correspond to the known binding site of BEAF-32 and a CACA-rich motif previously identified as enriched in regions bound by CP190.
source: The most enriched sequences correspond to the known binding site of BEAF-32 and to a CACA-rich motif previously identified as enriched in regions bound by CP190 (Nègre et al., 2010; Yang and Corces, 2012)
evidence: This claim is based on sequence analysis of boundary elements (Figure 4) and is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: The Zhimulev laboratory has identified interbands as a set of ~5700 short decompacted regions characterized by DNase hypersensitivity and the binding of characteristic proteins, including insulator proteins.
source: Using a combination of approaches, they have identified interbands as a set of ~5700 short decompacted regions that tend to be located near divergent promoters and are characterized by DNase hypersensitivity and the binding of characteristic proteins, including insulator proteins (Zhimulev et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Zhimulev et al., 2014.

claim: Vatolina et al., 2011a used electron microscopy to identify the fine banding pattern of the 65 kb region between polytene bands 10A1-2 and 10B1-2, revealing six discrete faint bands and seven interbands.
source: Vatolina et al., 2011a used exquisitely careful electron microscopy to identify the fine banding pattern of the 65 kb region between polytene bands 10A1-2 and 10B1-2, revealing that this region, which appears as a single interband under a light microscope, actually contains six discrete, faint bands and seven interbands.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Vatolina et al., 2011a.

claim: There is a striking correspondence between the polytene map assignments of Vatolina et al. and Hi-C data: faint polytene bands correspond to TADs, and interbands correspond to the boundary elements that separate the TADs.
source: There is a striking correspondence between the assignments of Vatolina et al. and our Hi-C data: faint polytene bands correspond to TADs, and interbands correspond to the boundary elements that separate the TADs.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of Hi-C data with polytene mapping data (Figure 5).

claim: 87.9% of representative boundaries show >2 fold enrichment for Chriz binding within 1.5 kb.
source: Using publicly available ChIP datasets from Kc167 cells (derived from late embryonic tissue), we observed a strong enrichment of Chriz binding at our representative boundaries (87.9% >2 fold enriched within 1.5 kb, Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of Chriz ChIP-seq data at boundaries (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A).

claim: The association between topological boundaries, insulator elements, and decompacted interband regions is proposed to be a general one that extends across the genome.
source: However, the combination of data from these loci with the close agreement of the molecular composition of these regions, specifically the strong localization of the interband marker Chriz to topological boundaries, leads us to propose that the precise relationship between topological boundaries, insulator elements, and decompacted interband regions we observe is a general one, and that it extends across the genome.
evidence: This is a proposed generalization based on the observed correspondence at specific loci and the enrichment of Chriz at boundaries.

claim: Insulators may function by increasing the physical distance between adjacent domains via the unpacking and extension of intervening chromatin.
source: The association between insulator binding and genomic regions with low compaction ratios suggests insulators may function by simply increasing the physical distance between adjacent domains via the unpacking and extension of intervening chromatin.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed association between insulators and low compaction regions.

claim: Hi-C data can resolve the borders of major polytene bands with precision.
source: We reasoned that if our Hi-C data is capable of resolving fine banding patterns such as that at the 10A1-B1 locus, we should be able to resolve the borders of major bands with precision.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the resolution demonstrated at the 10A1-B1 locus.

claim: A region of chromosome 2L that appeared as a single ~500 kb TAD at 15 kb resolution contains an intricate structure with two large TADs divided by a series of smaller domains.
source: We focused on a region of chromosome 2L that had previously been shown by Eagen et al. to appear as a single ~500 kb TAD using Hi-C at 15 kb resolution, but contains a faint interband in Bridge's map. Our Hi-C data reveal an intricate structure at this locus (Figure 6A). There are two large TADs on the left and right, divided by a series of smaller domains in the center.
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Hi-C data at high resolution (Figure 6A) and comparison to prior lower-resolution data.

claim: Hi-C signals at boundaries are virtually identical in anterior and posterior embryo halves.
source: Resulting Hi-C signals at boundaries are virtually identical in the two halves, despite substantially different gene expression profiles in these two embryonic regions (Figure 7A).
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of Hi-C data from anterior and posterior embryo halves (Figure 7A).

claim: Overall Hi-C signals are remarkably similar between anterior and posterior samples, with anterior and posterior samples correlating as strongly as replicates.
source: Indeed, overall Hi-C signals are remarkably similar, with anterior and posterior samples correlating as strongly as replicates.
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis of Hi-C data from anterior and posterior samples.

claim: Insulator boundary elements have nearly identical chromatin accessibility in anterior and posterior embryo halves as measured by ATAC-seq.
source: Analysis of ATAC-seq signal at insulator boundary elements in anterior and posterior halves showed that these elements have nearly identical accessibility in these two samples (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is based on ATAC-seq data from anterior and posterior embryo halves (Figure 7C).

claim: DNase-seq data from later embryonic stages show highly consistent profiles at boundaries.
source: Additionally, DNase-seq data from later embryonic stages that feature substantial tissue differentiation, transcription, and chromatin changes show highly consistent profiles at boundaries (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on DNase-seq data from multiple embryonic stages (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 1).

claim: Insulator-mediated chromatin organization is a constitutive feature of interphase chromatin of D. melanogaster embryos.
source: Together, these results are consistent with a model in which insulator-mediated chromatin organization is a constitutive feature of interphase chromatin of D. melanogaster embryos.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that boundaries and their accessibility are invariant across different embryonic regions and stages.

claim: Looping interactions between domain boundaries are not generally observed in Hi-C data.
source: In general, we do not observe looping interactions between domain boundaries in our Hi-C data.
evidence: This is a statement about the general absence of looping in the Hi-C data.

claim: 46 prominent examples of interactions between non-adjacent domains were noted during manual calling of topological boundaries.
source: However, during manual calling of topological boundaries for the entire genome, we noted 46 prominent examples of interactions between non-adjacent domains (Figure 8 and Figure 8—figure supplements 1–10, Supplementary file 1)
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of distal interactions identified by visual inspection.

claim: The Scr-ftz-Antp locus shows enriched contacts between the region containing the Scr promoter and a domain containing known Scr-targeting cis regulatory elements, while the ftz-containing domain makes minimal contact with its neighboring domains.
source: The most visually striking locus, which we emphasize was identified in an unbiased manner without knowing its identify, is the locus containing the Scr, ftz, and Antp genes (Figure 8A). This locus has been extensively studied, and a number of regulatory elements have been identified that reside between the ftz and Antp genes but 'skip' the ftz promoter to regulate Scr (Calhoun et al., 2002; Calhoun and Levine, 2003). Consistent with this, we observe enriched contacts between the region containing the Scr promoter and a domain on the other side of ftz that contains the known Scr-targeting cis regulatory elements, while the ftz-containing domain makes minimal contact with its neighboring domains.
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Hi-C data at the Scr-ftz-Antp locus (Figure 8A) and is supported by citations to prior studies of this locus.

claim: A loop brings together the promoters of knirps and the related knrl (knirps-like) genes.
source: As shown in Figure 8B, one of these loops brings together the promoters of knirps and the related knrl (knirps-like) genes.
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Hi-C data at the knirps-knrl locus (Figure 8B).

claim: Loops connect the achaete and scute genes.
source: Other loops connect the achaete and scute genes (Figure 8—figure supplement 3)
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Hi-C data at the achaete-scute locus (Figure 8—figure supplement 3).

claim: Loops connect sloppy paired 1 and sloppy paired 2.
source: sloppy paired 1 and sloppy paired 2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 4)
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Hi-C data at the sloppy paired locus (Figure 8—figure supplement 4).

claim: A loop connects the promoter of Ultrabithorax with an element in its first intron.
source: and the promoter of Ultrabithorax  with an element in its first intron (Figure 8—figure supplement 5).
evidence: This claim is based on visual inspection of Hi-C data at the Ultrabithorax locus (Figure 8—figure supplement 5).

claim: Many of the limited number of distal interactions observed involve genes that are transcriptionally active during stage 5 of embryogenesis.
source: Nevertheless, it is striking that of the limited number of distal interactions we observed, many of them involve genes that are transcriptionally active during stage 5 of embryogenesis.
evidence: This is an observation based on the identity of genes involved in distal interactions.

claim: Several Hi-C studies in flies have identified enrichments of insulator proteins at TAD boundaries.
source: Several Hi-C studies in flies have identified enrichments of insulator proteins at TAD boundaries (Sexton et al., 2012; Ulianov et al., 2016; Eagen et al., 2015; Mourad and Cuvier, 2016)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior Hi-C studies in Drosophila.

claim: There is a close, two-way association between sites of combinatorial insulator protein binding (insulators) and the boundaries between topological domains.
source: Rather, by using a combination of visual inspection of Hi-C maps at a large number of loci, unbiased hand-calling, and computational searches, we consistently observed a very close, two-way association between sites of combinatorial insulator protein binding (insulators) and the boundaries between topological domains.
evidence: This claim is based on the combined analysis of Hi-C data and insulator protein binding data using multiple approaches.

claim: Estimates suggest that there are ~5000 interbands constituting 5% of genomic DNA, with an average length of 2 kb.
source: First, estimates suggest that there are ~5000 interbands constituting 5% of genomic DNA, with an average length of 2 kb (Zhimulev, 1996; Vatolina et al., 2011a), numbers that are in line with our estimates of boundary element length and number.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior estimates of interband number and size.

claim: CP190 appears to be a constitutive feature of all or nearly all interbands.
source: Second, interbands are associated with insulator proteins, with CP190 appearing to be a constitutive feature of all or nearly all interbands (Pai et al., 2004; Gerasimova et al., 2007), which is precisely what we observe for boundary elements.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies of CP190 localization in polytene chromosomes.

claim: Interbands are highly sensitive to DNase digestion.
source: Third, interbands and boundary elements are highly sensitive to DNase digestion (Vatolina et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a prior study.

claim: Interbands contain the promoters and 5' ends of genes.
source: Fourth, interbands have been shown to contain the promoters and 5' ends of genes (Jamrich et al., 1977; Sass, 1982; Sass and Bautz, 1982a, 1982b; Rykowski et al., 1988)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Deletion of both isoforms of BEAF-32 results in polytene X chromosomes that exhibit loss of banding and are wider and shorter than wild type.
source: Finally, deletion of both isoforms of BEAF-32, the second-most highly enriched insulator protein at boundary elements, results in polytene X chromosomes that exhibit loss of banding and are wider and shorter than wild type, consistent with a loss of decompacted BEAF-32-bound regions (Roy et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to a genetic study.

claim: Decompacted insulator elements constitute a significant fraction of polytene interbands.
source: It is possible that interbands in polytene chromosomes result from multiple underlying molecular phenomena, but we believe it is likely that decompacted insulator elements constitute a significant fraction of these structures.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the observed correspondence between insulators and interbands and their shared molecular properties.

claim: The chromatin extension model of insulator function is not mutually exclusive with a role for looping in the function of some insulators.
source: While we and others have not observed frequent looping of insulators in Hi-C data from fly tissue, our model of chromatin compaction at insulators is not mutually exclusive with a role for looping in the function of some insulators.
evidence: This is a statement about the compatibility of the proposed model with other mechanisms.

claim: Interactions between boundaries seem to organize special genome structures with clear functional implications at the Scr locus.
source: Indeed, we have observed a limited set of cases in which interactions between boundaries seem to organize special genome structures with, at least in the case of the Scr locus, clear functional implications.
evidence: This claim is based on the observed looping at the Scr locus and its known regulatory function.

claim: Boundary-associated distal interactions are rare and do not appear to be general features of the function of boundary elements.
source: However, we emphasize that these interactions are rare and do not appear to be general features of the function of boundary elements.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the limited number of distal interactions observed in the Hi-C data.

claim: Interphase chromatin consists of alternating stretches of compacted, folded chromatin domains separated by regions of decompacted, stretched regions.
source: In this picture, interphase chromatin consists of alternating stretches of compacted, folded chromatin domains separated by regions of decompacted, stretched regions.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the observed correspondence between TADs, boundaries, bands, and interbands.

claim: Compacted regions vary in size from a few to hundreds of kilobases and correspond to both polytene band regions and TADs in Hi-C data.
source: The compacted regions vary in size from a few to hundreds of kilobases and correspond to both polytene band regions and TADs in Hi-C data.
evidence: This is a description of the proposed model based on the observed data.

claim: Decompacted regions that separate compacted domains are short DNA elements defined by the strong binding of insulator proteins and correspond to polytene interbands and TAD boundaries (insulators).
source: Decompacted regions that separate these domains are short DNA elements that are defined by the strong binding of insulator proteins and correspond to polytene interbands and TAD boundaries (insulators).
evidence: This is a description of the proposed model based on the observed data.

claim: Hi-C experiments were conducted using a modestly adapted version of the protocol described in Rao et al., 2014.
source: We prepared and sequenced in situ Hi-C libraries from two biological replicates of hand-sorted cellular blastoderm (mitotic cycle 14; mid-stage 5) embryos using a modestly adapted version of the protocol described in Rao et al., 2014.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methods used.

claim: Embryos were collected from OregonR strain D. melanogaster.
source: OregonR strain D. melanogaster (RRID:FlyBase_FBst1000080) embryos were collected on molasses plates seeded with fresh yeast paste from a population cage and aged to appropriate developmental stages, all at 25°C.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental materials and methods.

claim: Single-ends of demultiplexed reads were separately mapped using Bowtie to the D. melanogaster genome dm6 (R6.17).
source: Single-ends of demultiplexed reads were separately mapped using Bowtie (Langmead et al., 2009) (parameters: -m1 --best --strata) to the D. melanogaster genome dm6 (R6.17).
evidence: This is a statement about the computational methods used for data analysis.

claim: An iterative mapping procedure was used to map reads that failed to map uniquely due to chimeric junctions.
source: To address this, we used an iterative mapping procedure, in which we began by mapping the first 20 nt of the reads (using Bowtie's --trim3 feature). Unique mappings were kept, reads that failed to map were stored, and the procedure was repeated on the multiply-mapping reads, incrementing the length of sequence to map by 7 nt each round (attempt to uniquely map using first 20, first 27, first 34...).
evidence: This is a statement about the computational methods used for data analysis.

claim: The iterative mapping method gave 5–10% increases in yield of mapped reads over a procedure that explicitly detected and trimmed ligation junctions.
source: We found that this method gave 5–10% increases in yield of mapped reads over a procedure in which we attempted to explicitly detect and trim ligation junctions from reads.
evidence: This is a statement about the performance of the computational method.

claim: Local directionality scores were calculated for each 500 bp bin by summing the counts linking the bin to regions in a window encompassing the genomic regions between 1 and 15 kb from the bin upstream and downstream.
source: Local directionality scores were calculated for each bin by summing the counts linking the bin to regions in a window encompassing the genomic regions between 1 and 15 kb from the bin (skipping the two proximal 500 bp bins, summing the next 28) upstream and downstream, then taking the log (10) ratio of downstream to upstream.
evidence: This is a statement about the computational methods used for boundary detection.

claim: ATAC-seq was performed on pools of 20 anterior or posterior embryo halves.
source: We again sectioned embryos into anterior and posterior halves and performed ATAC-seq (Buenrostro et al., 2013) on pools of 20 embryo halves.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental methods used.

claim: All unique experiments were prepared in duplicate.
source: All unique experiments were prepared in duplicate.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental design.
